title: Late Is Wrong: The Reading and When It Was Taken

questions.question: A sensor reading arrives 20 ms after the moment it describes. Your code treats it as current. How wrong is the robot's position?
options: Speed times 20 ms, exactly: 2 cm at 1 m/s and nothing at all standing still
20 ms of the sensor's own noise
It depends on the controller gains
Nothing, if the loop runs faster than 50 Hz
questions.explanation: Measured across six speeds, the error matched speed times latency to within a nanometre every time. The zero at rest is why this passes every bench test.

questions.question: The loop from 14-04 settles in 1.2 s. Its measurement is made 0.06 s old, then 0.24 s old. What happens?
options: 0.06 s costs nothing at all; 0.24 s overshoots by 98 percent and it never settles
Both degrade it by about the same proportion
Both are fine, since the loop is much slower than either
0.06 s already destabilises it
questions.explanation: The failure arrives suddenly rather than gradually, in the same place the filter lag of 15-01 did: about a fifth of the settling time.

questions.question: A filter of 128 samples and a bus that is 63 samples late impose the same 0.126 s of lag. How do their effects on the loop compare?
options: Almost identically: 2.8 percent overshoot against 3.6 percent, and the same settling time
The filter is far worse, because it also distorts the signal
The bus delay is far worse, because it is a pure delay
They cannot be compared, as one is a filter
questions.explanation: The loop cannot tell where the lag came from. The difference between them is that the filter's window is a number in your code and the bus's latency is written down nowhere.

questions.question: The latency jitters between 4 and 36 ms, giving 2.2 cm rms of position error at 1 m/s. You smooth the readings over 16 samples. What do you measure?
options: 3.5 cm: worse, because the filter adds its own 15 ms of lag to the bus's 20
About 0.6 cm, the noise divided by four
About 2.2 cm, unchanged
About 1.1 cm, the noise halved
questions.explanation: It is not zero mean noise on the value, it is the value being about the wrong moment, and the average of a set of wrong moments is an older wrong moment.

questions.question: You carry a reading forward using a speed estimate that is 25 percent wrong. How much of the 2 cm error is left?
options: 25 percent of it, 5 mm: the leftover is the original error times how wrong the rate was
All of it, since the correction needs the true speed
None, the timestamp is what matters
More than 2 cm, because a wrong correction is worse than none
questions.explanation: There is no threshold below which compensating stops being worth doing. A rate estimate half wrong still removes half the problem.

questions.question: Your position error scatters by 2 cm. How do you tell latency jitter from sensor noise before changing anything?
options: Measure the scatter parked and again at 1 m/s: noise is the same in both, latency error grows with speed and vanishes at rest
Filter it and see whether the scatter falls as one over the square root of the window
Compare it against the sensor's datasheet figure
Check whether the readings are normally distributed
questions.explanation: The filtering test is worth knowing about but is not decisive here, since smoothing this error made it worse rather than leaving it unchanged.
